---
title: "Erosion control: GEP valuation and ecosystem-service shock"
format: html
---

## Purpose

This module does two things. The **GEP valuation** values the 2019 crop production that land cover
protects from water erosion, following the authors' write-up (`Soil_Erosion_Control.docx`, version
of 26 October 2026). The **shock** turns the pipeline's own 300 m SEALS land-use maps into a per-region, per-year **crop-productivity
shock** for the eight crop sectors (`PDR`, `WHT`, `GRO`, `V_F`, `OSD`, `C_B`, `PFB`, `OCR`), so the
economic model responds to the soil protection each scenario's land cover actually provides rather
than to a frozen table.

Land cover enters soil loss only through the cover-management factor, so scenario differences in this
module are land-driven by construction.

## GEP valuation

The account value is the crop production that vegetation and land cover protect from water erosion,
in constant 2019 USD. It is an intermediate service inside crop provision, reported separately and
not added to total GEP.

1. **Severe cropland.** Valuation counts only cropland pixels where modelled soil loss exceeds the
   country's threshold: 2 t/ha/yr for countries under 50,000 km² or with mean elevation below 250 m,
   and 11 t/ha/yr otherwise.
2. **Prevention shares.** On each severe cropland pixel, the on-farm share is
   $PS^{on} = AE / (AE + USLE)$, with $AE$ the erosion vegetation avoids and $USLE$ the soil loss that
   remains. The upstream share $PS^{up}$ is the same ratio of D8 flow-accumulated avoided and
   potential erosion from the land draining to the pixel. The two are combined using the bounded
   formula $PS^{comb} = 1 - (1 - PS^{on})(1 - PS^{up})$.
3. **Protected production.** Each crop's protected production is the prevention share times its
   SPAM2020 yield and harvested area, summed over the country's pixels.
4. **Shock.** A country's shock is protected production weighted by each crop's erosion-to-yield
   elasticity, over total production: $\text{Shock}_k = \sum_c PP_{c,k}\, \varepsilon_c / \sum_c
   \text{Prod}_{c,k}$. Elasticities follow Sartori et al. (2019), about 0.30 for cereals and 0.15 for
   roots, oilseeds and vegetables, with 0.08 where a crop has none.
5. **Value.** $\text{GEP}_k = \text{GPV}_k \times \text{Shock}_k$, with GPV the country's FAOSTAT crop
   gross production value in constant 2019 USD. GDP enters only to report the value as a share of
   GDP.

The three components (on-farm, upstream, combined) are computed side by side. The account reports
the combined one, summed to the account's r250 countries.

**Missing inputs.** A country without a crop gross production value or without a shock is missing,
not zero. A zero comes only from a present zero gross production value or a present zero shock.

**Fallback crop value.** The fallback works at the country total, not crop by crop. Where FAOSTAT
gives a country no crop gross production value at all, the whole country total is replaced by a
fallback total: producer price times quantity, summed over the country's crops, each crop priced at
the country's own price or else that crop's global mean price
(`load_fao_gpv_iso3_const2019_with_fallback` in `erosion_tasks.py`). The fallback values the same
crop items as the FAOSTAT totals, and a country with no valued crop row has no fallback total and
stays missing. A country that has a FAOSTAT total keeps it, and gaps inside it are not filled. The write-up describes a national, then regional
or global, price. The regional step is not in the code, a difference recorded for the authors, and
the code is unchanged.

**Repeated price rows.** The producer-price file lists some rows twice, identical in every column:
52 of Switzerland's rows and 28 of Serbia's. These exact repeats are dropped before the global mean
prices are taken, so each country's price counts once in the mean. Both countries have FAOSTAT
totals, so their own values do not use the fallback, but the repeats weighted their prices twice in
the means that fill other countries' missing prices. Dropping them lowers the combined value by
$30.89M across 55 countries, by at most 2.3% for any one country. The file also splits some records
over two rows, one with the crop name and one with the quantity. Those rows differ, are kept, and
value each such crop once.

**Crop items.** The FAOSTAT value table holds both crop and livestock items. The code keeps the
items of FAOSTAT's own "Crops" item group (value domain QV, group 2041, 160 items), chosen by item
code (`crop_item_codes` and `crop_items_only` in `erosion_functions.py`). A group total listed
among the members is left out, and a country that lists one crop twice stops the run. The authors'
code instead matches item names against a word list. That list misses many crops, among them sugar
cane, oranges, bananas, olives, sugar beet, tea and natural rubber, and its pattern "oat" also keeps
goat meat. On the reported FAOSTAT totals of 122 countries the word list keeps $2,324.72bn of 2019
value where the item group gives $2,926.95bn. Valued with the same shocks, the item group raises
the combined value from $18.24bn to $21.26bn. This difference from the authors' code is recorded
for them.

## Shock method

The biophysics is InVEST's Sediment Delivery Ratio model, run per scenario and anchor year. It yields
two rasters that everything downstream is built from: **USLE**, the soil loss under actual land cover,
and **RKLS**, the loss the same pixel would suffer bare. Their difference is the erosion the land cover
prevents.

Turning that into an economic shock needs a coefficient linking erosion to yield. No method avoids
this, so it is the key calibration for erosion regardless of which variant is used.

We report **two** formulations side by side, because they answer different questions and neither is
strictly better.

### A, "damage_area" (the conservative reading, the 8% approach)

Only *severe* erosion is assumed to harm yield. A pixel is severe where USLE exceeds 11 t/ha/yr.
Cropland is SEALS7 class 2, measured as the full-resolution cropland fraction of each cell. For each
zone,

$$\text{level}_A = -100 \times 0.08 \times p_{crop}, \qquad p_{crop} = \frac{\text{severe cropland area}}{\text{total cropland area}}$$

This is thresholded, binary, on-farm only, and weighted by cropland *area*. Because land cover carries
no crop detail, method A is necessarily **uniform across sectors**. It cannot tell wheat land from
vegetable land. It runs as `erosion_method = 'damage_area'` (the damage-seam section of `erosion_tasks.py`), and its
shock is the scenario's level minus the base scenario's level in 2023, not the contemporaneous
difference described below.

### B, "service" (the comprehensive reading)

All erosion prevention counts, everywhere on cropland, and off-site protection is included. The
prevention share combines the on-farm fraction $1 - \text{USLE}/\text{RKLS}$ with an upstream term
obtained by D8 flow-accumulating prevented and potential mass, so vegetation upslope is credited for
the sediment it stops reaching land below.

Two properties matter. The zone average is **magnitude-weighted**: it aggregates tonnes, not
percentages, as prevented over potential production-weighted mass. Without this, a pixel preventing
90 % of almost no erosion would count as much as one preventing 40 % of a great deal. And the
coefficient is **per crop**, so a crop's own erosion sensitivity is applied to its own prevention
share before production-weighting across crops.

$$\text{level}_B = 100 \sum_c w_c \, \alpha_c \, \frac{\text{prevented}_c}{\text{potential}_c} \Big/ \sum_c w_c$$

Because crops are mapped to GTAP sectors, B reports a **different shock per sector**: a zone eroding
mainly under cereals sends that signal to `GRO` rather than spreading it across all eight.

### Sign conventions

A measures damage borne and is negative. B measures protection delivered and is positive. The two
use different thresholds, weights and upstream terms, so their levels are not comparable, and each
method's shock is taken against its own baseline.

## From level to shock

Each level is already a percentage of crop productivity, so a shock is an **absolute** difference of
levels, not a relative change. The two families of methods difference against different references.

- Methods B and B-thresholded (`erosion_shock`) take each scenario's level minus the baseline
  scenario's level in the same year. The difference is zero at the base year and interpolated
  linearly between the 5-year anchors. The same table also carries `shock_pct_fixedbase`, the
  scenario's level minus the baseline's level in the base year, for comparison.
- Method A (`erosion_method = 'damage_area'`, `erosion_damage_shock`) takes the scenario's level,
  interpolated from the base-year level through the anchors, minus that fixed base-year level
  (`annual_damage_change`). Where a physical stress is set, it applies from its onset year.

The shock is then applied as a factor-productivity term (`afeall`).

## Crop coefficients

The per-crop coefficients come from a table of erosion-to-yield sensitivities keyed by FAO item names,
joined to IFPRI SPAM crop groups. The join is one-to-many in places, since SPAM's 46 groups are coarser
than FAO's item list, so a few resolutions are representative substitutions rather than exact matches
(all citrus through oranges, all temperate fruit through apples, pigeon pea through dry peas). Four
SPAM aggregates have no FAO counterpart and inherit their sector's mean. For other cereals that gives
0.30, matching every named cereal in the table.

## Static fallback

When a service is not listed in `dynamic_es`, the same seam grafts a static task that reads the frozen
per-scenario dependency table instead. That table carries a single 2050 endpoint computed on older land
cover, so intermediate years are a synthetic ramp rather than real per-year values, which is why the
dynamic path exists.

## Compute

The SDR model is multi-hour and memory-heavy per global map, so resolution follows the run modality:
a 6.45 km analysis grid locally, native SEALS resolution on a cluster. `run_erosion.py` runs the calculation
standalone, which is the practical way to iterate on it without invoking the economic model.

## Coverage

The saved local table is one row for each of the account's 250 countries, base year 2019, in constant 2019 USD. Of the 250, 161 carry a value, 21 are computed zeros, and 68 rows are missing, kept as missing rather than zero because an input carries no data for those countries. The combined value sums to $21.23bn. Ten of the missing rows (ALA, AND, ESH, GLP, GUF, LIE, MCO, MTQ, SMR, XKX) have a shock but no crop gross production value. A zero means the computation returned zero. A missing row means the data to compute one is absent.
